notes.front: What is Structured Query Language (SQL)?
notes.back: The standard, declarative language used to manage, query and change the data in relational databases.
notes.explanation: The study guide calls SQL the standard language for relational databases; NoSQL systems are named for not using it as their main query language.
notes.example: Like asking a librarian for ‘every Austen novel published before 1815’ instead of walking the shelves: `SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city = 'Leeds'`.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Key data management terms”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a relational database?
notes.back: A database that organises structured data into tables of rows and columns, with a predefined schema, keys linking tables, and SQL to manage it.
notes.explanation: The predefined schema and key-based relationships are what the study guide contrasts with the non-relational approach.
notes.example: Like a set of linked ledgers: an orders table whose customer number points to a row in the customers table.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Key data management terms”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a non-relational database?
notes.back: A database approach built for large volumes of rapidly changing data that doesn’t fit well into a relational database’s rigid table structure.
notes.explanation: The study guide defines it by what it escapes: the rigid, tabular structure of the relational model.
notes.example: Like a box of index cards where each card can carry different fields: a game that stores each player’s ever-changing inventory as its own record.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Key data management terms”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the term NoSQL mean?
notes.back: Database systems that do not use SQL as their primary query language, typically offering flexible schema models.
notes.explanation: The study guide adds that NoSQL systems often put availability and scalability ahead of strict consistency.
notes.example: Like a notebook with no printed columns, rather than a ledger: a shop stores product records whose fields vary from item to item.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Key data management terms”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is object storage?
notes.back: A storage architecture that manages data as objects in a flat address space rather than in a file hierarchy.
notes.explanation: The study guide calls it ideal for unstructured data at massive scale.
notes.example: Like a cloakroom that hands you a ticket for each coat instead of a set of nested drawers: each photo is stored whole and fetched by its name.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Key data management terms”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Cloud Storage?
notes.back: A scalable, managed Google Cloud service that stores data as objects in containers called buckets.
notes.explanation: Every bucket is associated with a project, and projects are grouped under an organisation.
notes.example: Like a warehouse of labelled crates: a museum keeps its scanned artworks as objects in a bucket for its website to fetch.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud Storage overview”, “How Cloud Storage works”
notes.evidence: Cloud Storage is a scalable and managed storage service offered by Google Cloud that lets you store data as objects in containers called buckets. All buckets are associated with a project, and you group your projects under an organization.

notes.front: What is Standard storage in Cloud Storage?
notes.back: The storage class best for frequently accessed (‘hot’) data and for data kept only briefly.
notes.explanation: Used in a region, it suits data kept in the same location as the compute resources that use it.
notes.example: Like the shelf by the till for items sold every hour: an online shop’s product photos, fetched on every page view.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Storage classes”, “Standard storage”
notes.evidence: Standard storage is best for data that is frequently accessed ("hot" data), as well as data that is stored for only brief periods of time. When used in a region, Standard storage is appropriate for storing data in the same location as Google Kubernetes Engine clusters or Compute Engine instances that use the data.

notes.front: What is Nearline storage in Cloud Storage?
notes.back: A storage class for data you plan to read or modify on average once a month or less.
notes.explanation: Google’s own illustration is a collection of files that keeps growing and is analysed once a month.
notes.example: Like a back room you visit now and then: a photographer’s finished shoots, reopened only when a client orders a reprint.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Storage classes”, “Nearline storage”
notes.evidence: Nearline storage is ideal for data you plan to read or modify on average once per month or less. For example, if you want to continuously add files to Cloud Storage and plan to access those files once a month for analysis, Nearline storage is a great choice.

notes.front: What is Coldline storage in Cloud Storage?
notes.back: A storage class for data you plan to read or modify at most once a quarter.
notes.explanation: For data kept purely for backup or archiving, Google says Archive storage is more cost-effective because its storage costs are the lowest.
notes.example: Like a basement store opened at each quarter’s audit: quarterly compliance extracts that are checked four times a year.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Storage classes”, “Coldline storage”
notes.evidence: Coldline storage is ideal for data you plan to read or modify at most once a quarter. Note, however, that for data being kept entirely for backup or archiving purposes, Archive storage is more cost-effective, as it offers the lowest storage costs.

notes.front: What is Archive storage in Cloud Storage?
notes.back: The lowest-cost, highly durable storage class, for data archiving, online backup and disaster recovery.
notes.explanation: Unlike the coldest services of some other cloud providers, its data is available within milliseconds, not hours or days.
notes.example: Like a sealed deed box in a solicitor’s strongroom: seven years of closed accounts kept in case an auditor ever asks.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Storage classes”, “Archive storage”
notes.evidence: Archive storage is the lowest-cost, highly durable storage service for data archiving, online backup, and disaster recovery. Unlike the "coldest" storage services offered by other Cloud providers, your data is available within milliseconds, not hours or days.

notes.front: What is Autoclass in Cloud Storage?
notes.back: A bucket feature that automatically moves each object to a suitable storage class based on that object’s access pattern.
notes.explanation: Data that isn’t accessed moves to colder classes to cut storage cost, and data that is accessed moves to Standard storage to speed future access.
notes.example: Like a warehouse that moves slow-selling stock to the back rooms by itself and brings items forward when someone asks for them.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Autoclass”
notes.evidence: The Autoclass feature automatically transitions objects in your bucket to appropriate storage classes based on each object's access pattern. The feature moves data that isn't accessed to colder storage classes to reduce storage cost and moves data that is accessed to Standard storage to optimize future accesses.

notes.front: What is Rapid storage in Cloud Storage?
notes.back: A high-performance storage class optimised for input/output-intensive workloads, storing data in zonal locations.
notes.explanation: Keeping objects in the same zones as the compute resources gives much lower latency and higher throughput than other classes.
notes.example: Like keeping the ingredients on the cook’s own worktop rather than in the pantry: training data stored in the very zone where the processing runs.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Storage classes”, “Rapid storage”
notes.evidence: Rapid storage is a high-performance storage class that's optimized for I/O-intensive workloads. When you use Rapid storage as a bucket's storage class, you can store your data in zonal locations. Storing your objects in the same zones as your compute resources enables significantly lower latency and higher throughput compared to other storage classes.

notes.front: What is Cloud SQL?
notes.back: A fully managed relational database service for MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server.
notes.explanation: Google says it frees you from database administration tasks so you have more time to manage your data.
notes.example: Like renting a serviced flat instead of maintaining a house: a web shop moves its MySQL database to Google Cloud and stops patching the server itself.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud SQL overview”
notes.evidence: Cloud SQL is a fully managed relational database service for MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server. This frees you from database administration tasks so that you have more time to manage your data.

notes.front: What is AlloyDB for PostgreSQL?
notes.back: A fully managed, PostgreSQL-compatible database service from Google Cloud.
notes.explanation: It pairs a Google-built database engine with a cloud-based, multi-node architecture for enterprise-grade performance, reliability and availability.
notes.example: Like a tuned-up version of a familiar car that still takes the same keys: a PostgreSQL application keeps its code but runs on a faster managed engine.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “AlloyDB overview”
notes.evidence: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL is a fully managed, PostgreSQL-compatible database service. It pairs a Google-built database engine with a cloud-based, multi-node architecture to deliver enterprise-grade performance, reliability, and availability for your most demanding applications.

notes.front: What is Spanner?
notes.back: A Google Cloud relational database service that offers both traditional relational structure and horizontal scalability.
notes.explanation: The study guide calls it Cloud Spanner; Google’s documentation and the exam guide call it Spanner.
notes.example: Like one shared ledger that many branches write to at once, and that grows by adding more clerks: a worldwide booking system that keeps one set of tables.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Google Cloud data management”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Bigtable?
notes.back: A Google Cloud database of sparsely populated, key-value tables that scale to billions of rows and thousands of columns, holding terabytes or petabytes.
notes.explanation: Google calls it ideal for large amounts of single-keyed data at low latency, with high read and write throughput.
notes.example: Like a vast tally sheet with one row per sensor and a column per minute: a power company’s smart-meter readings.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Bigtable overview”
notes.evidence: Bigtable is a sparsely populated table that can scale to billions of rows and thousands of columns, enabling you to store terabytes or even petabytes of data. Bigtable is ideal for storing large amounts of single-keyed data with low latency. It supports high read and write throughput at low latency,

notes.front: What is Firestore?
notes.back: An enterprise-grade, fully managed document database from Google Cloud.
notes.explanation: Google describes it as a highly available NoSQL database, with multi-region replication and advanced queries.
notes.example: Like a folder of forms where each form can have different fields: a fitness app stores each user’s profile and workouts as documents.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Firestore overview” (Firestore in Native mode)
notes.evidence: Firestore is an enterprise-grade, fully-managed document database from Google Cloud that offers multi-region data replication, advanced query capabilities, and ACID compliant transactions. With a 99.999% availability SLA, and disaster recovery features like managed backups, Firestore is a highly available NoSQL database that can support mission-critical workloads.

notes.front: What is BigQuery?
notes.back: A fully managed, AI-ready data platform for managing and analysing data, with built-in features such as machine learning and business intelligence.
notes.explanation: Its serverless architecture lets you use SQL and Python with zero infrastructure management.
notes.example: Like hiring a research department that answers any question about your records without you buying a single filing cabinet: a retailer queries ten years of sales in one statement.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “BigQuery overview”
notes.evidence: BigQuery is a fully managed, AI-ready data platform that helps you manage and analyze your data with built-in features like machine learning, search, geospatial analysis, and business intelligence. BigQuery's serverless architecture lets you use languages like SQL and Python to answer your organization's biggest questions with zero infrastructure management.

notes.front: What is Database Migration Service (DMS)?
notes.back: A Google Cloud service that migrates databases into Cloud SQL and AlloyDB for PostgreSQL.
notes.explanation: It streamlines networking, manages the initial snapshot and ongoing replication, and gives status updates throughout the migration.
notes.example: Like a removals firm that packs, moves and keeps forwarding your post until you switch over: a firm moves its on-premises MySQL database into Cloud SQL.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Database Migration Service overview”
notes.evidence: Database Migration Service helps you migrate your data to Google Cloud. The service supports database migrations into Cloud SQL and AlloyDB for PostgreSQL instances. Database Migration Service streamlines networking, manages the initial snapshot and ongoing replication, and provides status updates throughout the migration process.

notes.front: Where does Datastream appear in the Cloud Digital Leader study guide?
notes.back: As a Google Cloud tool named, with Database Migration Service, for a fully managed database migration.
notes.explanation: The guide says such a managed migration offloads maintenance, in contrast to a simple lift-and-shift.
notes.example: The guide says no more about it; recognise it as a Google Cloud migration tool when it appears beside Database Migration Service in an option.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Database migration and modernization”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does a relational database differ from a non-relational one?
notes.back: Relational databases use rigid tables with a predefined schema; non-relational ones handle large volumes of rapidly changing data that doesn’t fit that structure.
notes.explanation: The study guide defines the non-relational approach by contrast with the relational model’s tables.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Key data management terms”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which two of the data products in the study guide are described as NoSQL databases?
notes.back: Bigtable and Firestore.
notes.explanation: Spanner, Cloud SQL and AlloyDB are the relational ones in the same list.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Google Cloud data management”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A social app stores millions of user posts whose fields differ from post to post and change often. The team does not want a rigid table schema. Which kind of database fits the study guide’s descriptions?
notes.back: A: flexible schemas for large volumes of rapidly changing data.
notes.choices:
A) A NoSQL, non-relational database
B) A relational database with a fixed schema
C) Object storage in a file hierarchy
D) A data warehouse for reporting
notes.choicesExplained: B: a fixed, predefined schema is what the team wants to avoid. C: object storage uses a flat address space, not a file hierarchy, and is not a database. D: a warehouse is for analysis and reporting, not an app’s live records.
notes.explanation: The study guide says non-relational databases handle rapidly changing data that doesn’t fit rigid tables, and NoSQL offers flexible schema models.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Key data management terms”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which database query language does the study guide give as an example of an open standard?
notes.back: SQL.
notes.explanation: An open standard is a publicly available specification, the kind the guide says lets diverse systems communicate.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Open standard versus open source”, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What kind of data does the study guide say Cloud Storage is for?
notes.back: Unstructured data, such as images, videos and backups.
notes.explanation: Cloud Storage is an object storage service, and object storage suits unstructured data at massive scale.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Google Cloud data management”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A film archive must keep millions of digitised video files and scanned posters, each stored and retrieved whole. Which Google Cloud product fits best?
notes.back: B: object storage for unstructured data such as videos and images.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud SQL
B) Cloud Storage
C) Bigtable
D) Firestore
notes.choicesExplained: A: Cloud SQL is a relational database for structured tables. C: Bigtable is a NoSQL database for single-keyed data at scale, not whole files. D: Firestore is a document database for app data.
notes.explanation: The study guide describes Cloud Storage as an object storage service for unstructured data like images, videos, logs and backups.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Google Cloud data management”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What annual durability does Google give for every Cloud Storage class?
notes.back: 99.999999999% (eleven nines).
notes.explanation: Other features shared by every class include no minimum object size and low latency with no offline data retrieval.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Storage classes”, “Class descriptions”
notes.evidence: No minimum object size. - Worldwide accessibility and worldwide storage locations. - Low latency with no offline data retrieval. - High durability (99.999999999% annual durability).

notes.front: If you create a Cloud Storage bucket without choosing a default storage class, which class does it get?
notes.back: Standard storage.
notes.explanation: Changing a bucket’s default class later does not affect objects already in it.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Storage classes”
notes.evidence: If you don't specify a default storage class when you create a bucket, that bucket's default storage class is set to Standard storage. - Changing the default storage class of a bucket does not affect any of the objects that already exist in the bucket.

notes.front: Which Cloud Storage class has a 30-day minimum storage duration?
notes.back: A: Nearline storage.
notes.choices:
A) Nearline storage
B) Standard storage
C) Coldline storage
D) Archive storage
notes.choicesExplained: B: Standard storage has no minimum storage duration. C: Coldline’s minimum is 90 days. D: Archive’s minimum is 365 days.
notes.explanation: Google presents the 30-day minimum, slightly lower availability and access costs as the trade-offs for Nearline’s lower at-rest storage costs.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Storage classes”, “Nearline storage”
notes.evidence: Nearline storage is a better choice than Standard storage in scenarios where slightly lower availability, a 30-day minimum storage duration, and costs for data access are acceptable trade-offs for lowered at-rest storage costs.

notes.front: Which Cloud Storage class has a 90-day minimum storage duration?
notes.back: D: Coldline storage.
notes.choices:
A) Nearline storage
B) Archive storage
C) Standard storage
D) Coldline storage
notes.choicesExplained: A: Nearline’s minimum is 30 days. B: Archive’s minimum is 365 days. C: Standard storage has no minimum storage duration.
notes.explanation: Google names the 90-day minimum, slightly lower availability and higher access costs as the trade-offs for Coldline’s lower at-rest costs.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Storage classes”, “Coldline storage”
notes.evidence: Coldline storage is a better choice than Standard storage or Nearline storage in scenarios where slightly lower availability, a 90-day minimum storage duration, and higher costs for data access are acceptable trade-offs for lowered at-rest storage costs.

notes.front: Which Cloud Storage class has a 365-day minimum storage duration?
notes.back: D: Archive storage.
notes.choices:
A) Standard storage
B) Coldline storage
C) Nearline storage
D) Archive storage
notes.choicesExplained: A: Standard storage has no minimum storage duration. B: Coldline’s minimum is 90 days. C: Nearline’s minimum is 30 days.
notes.explanation: Google lists the 365-day minimum alongside higher costs for data access and operations as Archive storage’s trade-offs.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Storage classes”, “Archive storage”
notes.evidence: Archive storage also has higher costs for data access and operations, as well as a 365-day minimum storage duration.

notes.front: In Google’s table of Cloud Storage classes, which of the four main classes charges no retrieval fees?
notes.back: Standard storage.
notes.explanation: The table shows Standard with no minimum duration and no retrieval fee, while Nearline shows 30 days and a fee.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Storage classes”, “Available storage classes”
notes.evidence: Standard storage STANDARD None None - >99.99% in multi-regions and dual-regions - 99.99% in regions Nearline storage NEARLINE 30 days Yes

notes.front: Moving from Standard to Archive storage, how do storage costs and retrieval fees change, according to the study guide?
notes.back: Storage costs fall step by step while retrieval fees rise: none for Standard, highest for Archive.
notes.explanation: The guide describes Nearline as having a small retrieval fee and Coldline higher ones, with Archive at the top.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Cloud Storage classes”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For data you plan to access less than once a year, which Cloud Storage class does Google call the best choice?
notes.back: Archive storage.
notes.explanation: Nearline suits roughly monthly access and Coldline at most quarterly access, leaving the rarest access to Archive.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Storage classes”, “Archive storage”
notes.evidence: Archive storage is the best choice for data that you plan to access less than once a year.

notes.front: A museum keeps high-resolution scans of its collection in Cloud Storage; curators pull a handful for the monthly newsletter and otherwise leave them untouched. Which storage class does Google suggest?
notes.back: B: Nearline storage suits data read about once a month or less.
notes.choices:
A) Archive storage
B) Nearline storage
C) Standard storage
D) Coldline storage
notes.choicesExplained: A: Archive is for data accessed less than once a year, and would add high access costs. C: Standard suits frequently accessed data and costs more to store. D: Coldline suits access at most once a quarter.
notes.explanation: Google calls Nearline ideal for data you plan to read or modify on average once per month or less.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Storage classes”, “Nearline storage”
notes.evidence: Nearline storage is ideal for data you plan to read or modify on average once per month or less.

notes.front: A pharmacy chain must keep dispensing extracts that auditors check once each quarter. Which storage class fits best?
notes.back: B: Coldline storage suits data read at most once a quarter.
notes.choices:
A) Standard storage
B) Coldline storage
C) Rapid storage
D) Archive storage
notes.choicesExplained: A: Standard storage is for frequently accessed data and costs most to store. C: Rapid storage is for high-performance, input/output-intensive work. D: Archive is for data accessed less than once a year.
notes.explanation: Google describes Coldline as ideal for data you plan to read or modify at most once a quarter.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Storage classes”, “Coldline storage”
notes.evidence: Coldline storage is ideal for data you plan to read or modify at most once a quarter.

notes.front: A law firm must keep closed case files for ten years to satisfy regulators, and expects to open almost none of them. Which storage class fits best?
notes.back: C: Archive storage, the lowest-cost class, for data accessed less than once a year.
notes.choices:
A) Standard storage
B) Nearline storage
C) Archive storage
D) Coldline storage
notes.choicesExplained: A: Standard is for frequently accessed data. B: Nearline suits roughly monthly access and costs more to store. D: Coldline suits quarterly access; for pure archiving Google says Archive is more cost-effective.
notes.explanation: Google gives data stored for legal or regulatory reasons as a use for Archive storage: low cost, yet still available if needed.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Storage classes”, “Archive storage”
notes.evidence: Archived data, such as data stored for legal or regulatory reasons, can be stored at low cost as Archive storage, yet still be available if you need it.

notes.front: A news site serves the same photos thousands of times an hour to readers around the world. Which storage class fits best?
notes.back: B: Standard storage, for frequently accessed ‘hot’ data.
notes.choices:
A) Coldline storage
B) Standard storage
C) Nearline storage
D) Archive storage
notes.choicesExplained: A: Coldline suits data read at most quarterly and charges for retrieval. C: Nearline suits roughly monthly access and charges for retrieval. D: Archive is for data accessed less than once a year.
notes.explanation: In a multi-region, Google says Standard storage suits data accessed around the world, such as serving website content.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Storage classes”, “Standard storage”
notes.evidence: When used in a multi-region, Standard storage is appropriate for storing data that is accessed around the world, such as serving website content, streaming videos, executing interactive workloads, or serving data supporting mobile and gaming applications.

notes.front: With Autoclass enabled, which storage class do newly added objects start in?
notes.back: Standard storage, even if the request specifies a different class.
notes.explanation: Autoclass manages all aspects of storage classes for the bucket, overriding the class named in the request.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Autoclass”, “Overview”
notes.evidence: When enabled, Autoclass manages all aspects of storage classes for a bucket: - All objects added to the bucket begin in Standard storage, even if a different storage class is specified in the request.

notes.front: By default, what is Autoclass’s terminal storage class, and what can you configure it to be instead?
notes.back: Nearline storage by default; optionally Archive storage.
notes.explanation: Objects move to the terminal class and stay there until they are accessed.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Autoclass”, “Overview”
notes.evidence: By default, the terminal storage class for Autoclass is Nearline storage, which means objects transition to Nearline storage and remain in that storage class until they're accessed. Optionally, you can configure Autoclass so that the terminal storage class is Archive storage.

notes.front: Under Autoclass, what happens to objects smaller than 128 KiB?
notes.back: They never move to colder classes; they stay in Standard storage permanently.
notes.explanation: Only an object’s data, not its metadata, counts towards the 128 KiB size.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Autoclass”, “Overview”
notes.evidence: Objects smaller than 128 KiB don't transition to colder storage classes. Instead, they are permanently stored in Standard storage. Only object data, not object metadata, is considered when determining whether the object is smaller than 128 KiB.

notes.front: For which two general access patterns does Google say Autoclass is useful?
notes.back: Data with a variety of access frequencies, and data whose access patterns are unknown or unpredictable.
notes.explanation: It is not recommended when most of a bucket’s data clearly fits the use case of a specific storage class.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Autoclass”, “Should you use Autoclass?”
notes.evidence: Your data has a variety of access frequencies. - The access patterns for your data are unknown or unpredictable. However, Autoclass isn't recommended if the majority of your bucket's data fits into the use cases of specific storage classes.

notes.front: A start-up’s bucket holds user uploads: some are opened daily, others never again, and nobody can predict which. The team wants storage costs cut without managing classes by hand. What should it enable?
notes.back: C: Autoclass moves objects between classes by their access patterns.
notes.choices:
A) Coldline storage as the default class
B) Rapid storage
C) Autoclass on the bucket
D) A 365-day minimum storage duration
notes.choicesExplained: A: a fixed Coldline default would charge for retrieving the daily-used files. B: Rapid storage is for high-performance zonal workloads, not cost cutting. D: a minimum storage duration is a condition of a class, not a feature you enable.
notes.explanation: Google recommends Autoclass for data with varied access frequencies or access patterns that are unknown or unpredictable.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Autoclass”, “Should you use Autoclass?”
notes.evidence: Your data has a variety of access frequencies. - The access patterns for your data are unknown or unpredictable.

notes.front: With which kind of bucket is the Rapid storage class compatible?
notes.back: Only zonal buckets, through Rapid Bucket.
notes.explanation: Google suggests it for the most data-intensive uses, such as artificial intelligence, machine learning and data analytics.
notes.source: Google Cloud, Cloud Storage documentation, “Storage classes”, “Rapid storage”
notes.evidence: This approach makes Rapid storage ideal for your most data-intensive use cases, such as Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and data analytics. Rapid storage is only compatible with zonal buckets through Rapid Bucket.

notes.front: What are two operations Cloud SQL handles so you don’t have to build and maintain them?
notes.back: Any two, among others: backups, high availability and failover, and maintenance and updates.
notes.explanation: Google’s list also includes network connectivity, export and import, monitoring and logging.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud SQL overview”, “What Cloud SQL provides”
notes.evidence: Cloud SQL offers many services so you don't have to build and maintain them yourself. You can focus on your data and let Cloud SQL handle the following operations: - Backups - High availability and failover - Network connectivity - Export and import - Maintenance and updates - Monitoring - Logging

notes.front: A travel agency runs its booking system on a PostgreSQL database on its own server. It wants to keep a standard relational PostgreSQL database but stop handling backups, patching and failover itself. Which product fits most simply?
notes.back: D: a fully managed relational database service for PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server.
notes.choices:
A) Firestore
B) Bigtable
C) Cloud Storage
D) Cloud SQL
notes.choicesExplained: A: Firestore is a NoSQL document database. B: Bigtable is a NoSQL database, not a PostgreSQL service. C: Cloud Storage holds objects, not a relational database.
notes.explanation: Google says Cloud SQL is a cloud-based alternative to local MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server databases for teams that want to spend less time managing the database.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud SQL overview”, “Use cases for Cloud SQL”
notes.evidence: Cloud SQL provides a cloud-based alternative to local MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server databases. You should use Cloud SQL if you want to spend less time managing your database and more time using it.

notes.front: What does AlloyDB’s columnar engine do?
notes.back: It accelerates analytical queries.
notes.explanation: It is part of AlloyDB’s query optimisation, alongside an index advisor that suggests schema improvements.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “AlloyDB overview”, “What AlloyDB provides”
notes.evidence: Query optimization: improve database performance using an index advisor that suggests schema improvements and a columnar engine that accelerates analytical queries.

notes.front: A logistics firm has a large, demanding PostgreSQL application. It wants to keep PostgreSQL compatibility, get enterprise-grade performance and availability, and speed up analytical queries on the same data. Which product fits best?
notes.back: A: fully managed and PostgreSQL-compatible, built for demanding applications.
notes.choices:
A) AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
B) Cloud Storage
C) Bigtable
D) Firestore
notes.choicesExplained: B: Cloud Storage stores objects, not a PostgreSQL database. C: Bigtable is a NoSQL database for single-keyed data. D: Firestore is a NoSQL document database, not PostgreSQL.
notes.explanation: Google describes AlloyDB as PostgreSQL-compatible, delivering enterprise-grade performance, reliability and availability for the most demanding applications.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “AlloyDB overview”
notes.evidence: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL is a fully managed, PostgreSQL-compatible database service. It pairs a Google-built database engine with a cloud-based, multi-node architecture to deliver enterprise-grade performance, reliability, and availability for your most demanding applications.

notes.front: A global ticketing platform needs a relational database with tables and consistent transactions, but its load outgrows a single server and must scale out horizontally. Which product does the study guide describe for this?
notes.back: D: relational structure combined with horizontal scalability.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud Storage
B) Firestore
C) Bigtable
D) Spanner
notes.choicesExplained: A: Cloud Storage is object storage, not a relational database. B: Firestore is a NoSQL document database. C: Bigtable is NoSQL, without relational tables.
notes.explanation: The study guide describes Spanner as a relational database service offering both traditional relational structure and horizontal scalability.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Google Cloud data management”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For data that must withstand the extended loss of an entire region, what are two managed, multi-regional storage services Google suggests?
notes.back: Any two, among others: Cloud Storage, Firestore and Spanner.
notes.explanation: Google gives these as a data strategy for applications built to recover from disasters.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Geography and regions”, “Application deployment considerations”
notes.evidence: To build disaster recovery capable applications that can withstand the extended loss of entire regions For data, use one or more of the following strategies: - Use managed, multi-regional storage services such as Cloud Storage, Datastore, Firestore, or Spanner.

notes.front: What are two types of data Google lists as suited to Bigtable?
notes.back: Any two, among others: time-series data, marketing data, and financial data.
notes.explanation: Google’s list continues with Internet of Things data and graph data.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Bigtable overview”, “What it's good for”
notes.evidence: You can use Bigtable to store and query all of the following types of data: - Time-series data, such as CPU and memory usage over time for multiple servers. - Marketing data, such as purchase histories and customer preferences. - Financial data, such as transaction histories, stock prices, and currency exchange rates.

notes.front: An energy company collects a reading every minute from millions of smart meters and needs very high write throughput with low-latency lookups by meter. Which product fits best?
notes.back: D: a NoSQL database for high-throughput, low-latency key-value data such as Internet of Things readings.
notes.choices:
A) Firestore
B) Cloud SQL
C) Archive storage
D) Bigtable
notes.choicesExplained: A: Firestore is a document database aimed at app development. B: Cloud SQL is a relational database for MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server, not built for billions of meter readings. C: Archive storage is for data accessed less than once a year.
notes.explanation: Google names Internet of Things data, such as usage reports from energy meters, among the data Bigtable is for.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Bigtable overview”, “What it's good for”
notes.evidence: Internet of Things data, such as usage reports from energy meters and home appliances.

notes.front: What does Firestore offer so that existing MongoDB applications can use it?
notes.back: A MongoDB-compatible interface, alongside its own client libraries.
notes.explanation: Google adds that Firestore also supports, but doesn’t require, integration with the Firebase app development platform.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Firestore overview” (Firestore in Native mode)
notes.evidence: In addition to idiomatic Firestore client libraries, Firestore also provides a MongoDB-compatible API that lets you use Firestore with existing MongoDB applications. Firestore also supports (but doesn't require) integration with the Firebase mobile and web app development platform.

notes.front: A start-up is building a mobile and web app whose user profiles and settings vary from user to user. It wants a flexible, scalable NoSQL document database with no servers to provision. Which product fits best?
notes.back: B: a fully managed, serverless NoSQL document database that scales automatically with load.
notes.choices:
A) Spanner
B) Firestore
C) BigQuery
D) Cloud SQL
notes.choicesExplained: A: Spanner is relational, with fixed table structure. C: BigQuery is a data warehouse for analysis, not an app’s live records. D: Cloud SQL is a relational database service.
notes.explanation: Google says Firestore needs no pre-provisioning of resources and scales automatically to match load, which suits app data whose fields vary from user to user.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Firestore overview” (Firestore in Native mode), “Key capabilities”
notes.evidence: Firestore uses a pay-per-use model. Firestore does not require any pre-provisioning of resources and auto scales to match your load.

notes.front: How does Google say you should port a legacy Datastore app to Firestore?
notes.back: Use Firestore with Datastore compatibility and the Datastore client libraries.
notes.explanation: Datastore compatibility is an interface layer on Firestore; beyond better App Engine integration, it offers no benefits over using Firestore directly.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Firestore overview” (Firestore in Native mode), “How do I port a legacy Datastore app to use Firestore?”
notes.evidence: Use Firestore with Datastore compatibility and the Datastore client libraries. Datastore compatibility mode supports legacy applications built on Datastore and App Engine. Datastore compatibility is an API layer on top of Firestore with the same availability, performance, consistency, and scalability. Beyond better integration with App Engine, Datastore compatibility doesn't offer any benefits over using Firestore directly.

notes.front: Into which two parts is BigQuery’s architecture divided?
notes.back: A storage layer and a compute layer, which operate independently of each other.
notes.explanation: Google’s petabit-scale network carries the communication between the two layers.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “BigQuery overview”
notes.evidence: BigQuery's architecture consists of two parts: a storage layer that ingests, stores, and optimizes data and a compute layer that provides analytics capabilities. These compute and storage layers efficiently operate independently of each other thanks to Google's petabit-scale network that enables the necessary communication between them.

notes.front: A retail group wants to run SQL analysis over years of sales from every region, measured in petabytes, without provisioning or scaling any servers. Which product fits best?
notes.back: D: a serverless, highly scalable data warehouse for analysis.
notes.choices:
A) Cloud SQL
B) Nearline storage
C) Firestore
D) BigQuery
notes.choicesExplained: A: Cloud SQL is a managed relational database for applications, not a petabyte-scale warehouse. B: Nearline is a storage class, not an analysis engine. C: Firestore is a document database for apps.
notes.explanation: Google says BigQuery can query terabytes in seconds and petabytes in minutes, with zero infrastructure management.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “BigQuery overview”
notes.evidence: BigQuery's scalable, distributed analysis engine lets you query terabytes in seconds and petabytes in minutes.

notes.front: What two broad ways does the study guide describe for migrating or modernising a database?
notes.back: A simple lift-and-shift for minimal upheaval, or a fully managed migration with tools such as Database Migration Service and Datastream.
notes.explanation: The managed route is the one the guide links to offloading maintenance.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Exploring Data Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Database migration and modernization”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A manufacturer runs a self-hosted MySQL database on virtual machines and wants to move it to Google Cloud while handing off the database’s day-to-day maintenance. Which approach fits?
notes.back: C: a migration to a managed database service offloads the maintenance.
notes.choices:
A) Keep it on-premises and add bandwidth
B) Copy the database files into Archive storage
C) Move it into Cloud SQL with Database Migration Service
D) Rebuild it as a data lake
notes.choicesExplained: A: staying on-premises moves nothing and keeps the maintenance in-house. B: Archive storage keeps files cheaply but does not run a database. D: a data lake stores raw data; it does not replace a running database.
notes.explanation: Google lists moving from self-hosted databases on virtual machines to managed database services as a Database Migration Service use case, freeing teams from managing the infrastructure.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Database Migration Service overview”, “Use cases”
notes.evidence: As part of an organization's move to Google Cloud, you can move from VM-based self-hosted databases to managed database cloud services. This lets you focus on the high availability, disaster recovery, and performance of running databases on managed services, instead of managing the infrastructure.

notes.front: In Database Migration Service, how does a continuous migration differ from a one-time migration?
notes.back: Continuous migration keeps replicating changes after an initial dump and load, allowing minimal downtime; one-time migration is a single point-in-time snapshot.
notes.explanation: During a one-time migration dependent applications can face downtime, because the source database can take no new writes while it runs.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Database Migration Service overview”, “Migration types”
notes.evidence: A one-time migration is a single point-in-time snapshot of the database. Database Migration Service takes the snapshot from the source and applies it to the destination. This process is a dump and load, where the destination is ready to be used when the load completes. Any applications that depend on the source database can experience downtime during the migration process

notes.front: An online retailer is moving its order database to Cloud SQL and cannot stop taking orders for more than a few minutes. Which Database Migration Service migration type fits?
notes.back: A: changes keep flowing until the switch, giving minimal downtime.
notes.choices:
A) Continuous migration
B) One-time migration
C) A snapshot copied to Coldline storage
D) No migration: add a zone instead
notes.choicesExplained: B: a one-time migration blocks new writes to the source while it runs, causing downtime. C: a stored snapshot is not a running database. D: adding a zone does not move the database.
notes.explanation: Continuous migration follows an initial dump and load with a continuous flow of changes; switching when source and destination are in sync gives minimal downtime.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Database Migration Service overview”, “Continuous migration”
notes.evidence: Continuous (sometimes referred to as ongoing or online) migration is a continuous flow of changes from your source to your destination that follows an initial full dump and load.

notes.front: What is the difference between a homogeneous and a heterogeneous database migration?
notes.back: Homogeneous moves data between the same database technology; heterogeneous moves it between different technologies.
notes.explanation: Google’s example of a heterogeneous migration is Oracle to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Database Migration Service overview”, “Migration types”
notes.evidence: Unlike homogeneous migrations, in heterogeneous migrations, such as Oracle to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL, the database technology of the source and destination are different.
